items.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini 3.7 Flash, an improved AI model for coding and agents with better accuracy and lower cost [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Introducing Gemini 3.7 Flash
items.summary:
Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 3.7 Flash, an upgraded AI model designed to enhance coding, knowledge work, and web development workflows. This model offers improved debugging, higher code accuracy, and better performance in generating production-ready code, while reducing costs to half of its predecessor, Gemini 3.6 Flash.

Gemini 3.7 Flash also improves developer experience by adapting better to challenges and following instructions more precisely, enabling more efficient multi-step planning and tool use. It is integrated into Gemini Spark, Google's personal AI agent, to enhance productivity in Google Workspace apps. The model includes updated safety safeguards against misuse in sensitive domains and is available to developers, enterprises, and individuals through various Google platforms.

items.title: Cerebras and OpenAI launch Ultrafast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol, delivering up to 750 tokens per second with no quality loss, initially for select customers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast
items.summary:
Cerebras and OpenAI have introduced Ultrafast mode for GPT-5.6 Sol, a new service tier in the OpenAI API that accelerates output speeds up to 750 tokens per second without compromising quality. This mode is initially available to select customers and aims to support time-sensitive, mission-critical applications by resolving the traditional tradeoff between speed and intelligence in AI models.

Benchmark tests show GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast answered 2,500 challenging questions in just over 11 hours, nearly seven times faster than comparable models, while maintaining accuracy. Powered by Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine architecture, Ultrafast mode reduces data movement bottlenecks common in GPU inference, enabling faster responses for applications such as legal briefs, financial models, and engineering reports.

Ultrafast mode is designed to enhance workflows where rapid AI inference is critical, including real-time incident response and cybersecurity. It allows organizations to deploy AI agents that keep pace with human thinking and collaboration, potentially transforming productivity and enabling new modes of working with AI.

items.title: Developer builds a home AI system using repurposed server GPUs and salvaged PC parts amid hardware shortages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI At Home Part 1: A Box Of Scraps
items.summary:
A software developer describes assembling a personal AI computing setup at home using overproduced AMD server GPUs originally intended for cloud gaming, combined with salvaged PC components due to current hardware shortages. The project aims to create a local AI data center to avoid reliance on external cloud services and maintain control over the technology.

The build includes four AMD V620 GPUs with 32GB VRAM each, an Intel Core i9 10900X CPU, and a motherboard with four PCIe x16 slots, all sourced from used or surplus hardware markets. Custom cooling solutions were designed and 3D-printed to address the lack of built-in fans on the server GPUs, enabling efficient airflow for the stacked cards. This approach reflects a practical and cost-conscious method to enable AI workloads at home despite the high cost and scarcity of new AI-optimized hardware.

items.title: Researchers introduce MBA-Bench, a multimodal benchmark and agents for business ideation using visual and textual data across six domains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MBA: Multimodal Benchmark and Agents for Real-World Business Ideation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed MBA-Bench, the first multimodal benchmark designed to train and evaluate business ideation agents using both visual and textual inputs. The benchmark includes 30,000 samples across six domains, each with unique visual cues that text alone cannot fully capture, and uses GPT-4o to generate reference ideas for business questions. Two agent models, MBA-b and MBA-k, are trained with novel reward objectives focusing on creativity and feasibility, outperforming baseline models by significant margins in extensive experiments.

MBA-Bench evaluates agents on six business-oriented criteria using a multimodal large language model as a judge, with MBA-b handling blind criteria settings and MBA-k optimizing known criteria. Training involves LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning followed by group relative policy optimization. The multimodal agents approach the performance of closed-source models on several metrics, demonstrating the value of integrating visual information for real-world business ideation tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11616v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agentic systems powered by large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities for business ideation. Yet existing approaches remain confined to a text-only paradigm, despite the inherently multimodal nature of real-world contexts. We thus introduce MBA-Bench, the first multimodal benchmark for training and evaluating business ideation agents, comprising 30K samples across six domains, each domain characterized by distinct visual cues not fully conveyed by text alone. Concretely, we automatically caption images and employ GPT-4o to generate five reference ideas for each of three business questions through retrieval query generation, market evidence retrieval, and evidence-augmented synthesis. Following prior work, we evaluate agents across six business-oriented criteria using MLLM-as-a-Judge. To consider settings where criteria are hidden or disclosed, we present MBA-b and MBA-k for blind and known, respectively. We train both with two novel reward objectives---creativity and feasibility---while MBA-k further optimizes the six disclosed criteria for eight in total. Both are trained via LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning followed by group relative policy optimization with these setting-specific rewards. For extensive experiments on MBA-Bench, we set up two baselines accommodating either captions only or multimodal inputs, with the latter nearing closed-source performance on several metrics. MBA-b and MBA-k outperform caption baselines by 63.9% and 77.1%, and multimodal baselines by 25.6% and 35.8%, respectively.

items.title: Researchers propose REOPD, a reliability-adaptive reward extrapolation method for on-policy distillation that improves training stability and performance across multiple domains without extra models or rollouts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: REOPD: Reliability-Adaptive Reward Extrapolation for On-Policy Distillation
items.summary:
REOPD is a new framework for on-policy distillation that adjusts reward extrapolation at the token level using a compatibility weight combined with a batch-level adaptive budget. This approach preserves alignment with the teacher model while selectively amplifying reliable signals, avoiding reward hacking and unstable training caused by global coefficients. The method requires no additional verifier, reward model, value model, or rollouts beyond standard on-policy distillation.

In experiments, REOPD outperforms previous methods like G-OPD on single-teacher mathematics tasks and multi-teacher settings, while matching performance on single-teacher code tasks. This demonstrates its ability to adapt reward extrapolation finely across different domains and teacher configurations, reducing the need for costly hyperparameter tuning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.11698v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own trajectories under dense token-level supervision from a teacher. Reward-extrapolation methods such as ExOPD amplify the teacher-reference log-likelihood ratio to move beyond direct imitation, but apply a single global coefficient $\lambda$ to every token. This can drive the student to fit extreme peaks in the implicit reward, causing reward hacking and unstable training, and the optimal $\lambda$ varies across domains, requiring costly sweeps. We propose REOPD, a reliability-adaptive reward extrapolation framework for OPD. REOPD combines a token-level compatibility weight with a batch-level adaptive budget, yielding a token-wise coefficient $\lambda_{b,t}=1+\gamma_b q_t$ that preserves teacher alignment while selectively extrapolating along reliable teacher-reference directions. It requires no verifier, reward model, value model, or extra rollout beyond standard OPD. REOPD outperforms G-OPD on single-teacher mathematics and on both domains in the multi-teacher setting, while matching G-OPD on single-teacher code, demonstrating effective fine-grained reliability adaptation across domains and teacher configurations.

items.title: Researchers identify Information Abundance Paradox where longer training contexts reduce parametric knowledge in large language models, impacting performance and robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Information Abundance Paradox: Long-Context Training Undermines Parametric Knowledge
items.summary: Researchers propose the Information Abundance Paradox, showing that training large language models with longer context windows can decrease the models' parametric knowledge by increasing reliance on context. Their study finds that while longer contexts initially improve language modeling and understanding, performance declines beyond an optimal context length, and fine-tuning with more context reduces robustness when context is missing or misleading at test time. The shift in learning dynamics moves gradient pressure from feed-forward networks to attention modules, suggesting that simply scaling context length is not a straightforward path to better model knowledge retention or inference.
items.description: Researchers propose the Information Abundance Paradox, showing that training large language models with longer context windows can decrease the models' parametric knowledge by increasing reliance on context. Their study finds that while longer contexts initially improve language modeling and understanding, performance declines beyond an optimal context length, and fine-tuning with more context reduces robustness when context is missing or misleading at test time. The shift in learning dynamics moves gradient pressure from feed-forward networks to attention modules, suggesting that simply scaling context length is not a straightforward path to better model knowledge retention or inference.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12218v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models are increasingly trained and deployed with long contexts that span documents, code repositories, and interaction histories. This scaling reflects the implicit assumption that training on longer contexts will only help the model by exposing it to richer evidence. We challenge this view by studying how the context window shapes a model's mode of learning, shifting it between parametric internalization and contextualization. We propose the Information Abundance Paradox, which hypothesizes that abundant relevant information in the training context can reduce the incentive to encode that information parametrically, thereby increasing reliance on context. In pretraining with long documents, increasing the context window improves language modeling, natural language understanding, and closed-book MCQA only up to an intermediate optimum, after which performance consistently declines. In supervised fine-tuning, more task-relevant train-time context improves performance with supporting context, but reduces robustness when context is absent or misleading at test time. Our analysis suggests that this behavior arises when longer context provides a lower complexity solution. Mechanistically, training with informative context shifts gradient pressure from feed-forward networks, often linked to parametric knowledge, toward attention modules, and causal interventions show that this shift increases reliance on context during inference. Overall, these findings support the Information Abundance Paradox and suggest that scaling toward near-infinite context is not simply a matter of supplying more data, even when high-quality long-context data is abundant.

items.title: Researchers introduce Causal Attribution Score (CAS) for local and global causal explanations in AI, outperforming traditional methods in benchmarks and empirical datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CAS: A Causal Attribution Score for Local and Global Explainable Artificial Intelligence
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Causal Attribution Score (CAS), a method that provides causal explanations for AI model outputs by attributing intervention effects on real-world outcomes. CAS uses an interventional coalition game framework with causal Shapley contributions to generate local and global causal explanations, distinguishing causal effect heterogeneity from mere outcome prediction.

Benchmark tests with simulated data showed CAS achieves lower mean absolute error compared to traditional normalization methods, especially under strong interactions. Empirical analyses on datasets involving 401(k) eligibility and unemployment benefits revealed that CAS rankings of treatment-effect modifiers differ significantly from predictive SHAP rankings, highlighting the importance of separating causal explanations from predictive importance in AI models.

items.originalTitle: Dead text or binding clause? Measuring and restoring constraint influence in black-box LLM dialogues
items.summary:
A recent study presents a system that addresses "behavioral relapse" in multi-turn dialogues with large language models (LLMs), where models continue to follow revoked constraints. The system uses a contract ledger to track constraints and revocations, measures adherence per clause, and applies repairs within resource limits, making revocation failure measurable and manageable.

Experiments show that stronger models exhibit less relapse, and the proposed methods significantly reduce constraint violations compared to baseline approaches. The system can predict relapse before response delivery and partially recover from it with simple interventions, improving dialogue state management in LLM interactions.

items.title: Researchers introduce SteerBench-Work, a benchmark for evaluating AI agent decisions to proceed or hold actions across workplace domains using 106 incident-based scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SteerBench-Work: A Benchmark for Agent Steering at Action Boundaries
items.summary:
SteerBench-Work is a new benchmark designed to assess how long-running large language model (LLM) agents decide whether to proceed with or hold actions at critical boundaries in workplace settings such as developer operations, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, and security. The benchmark includes 106 scenarios based on public incidents, with balanced labels for proceed and hold decisions, allowing models to be scored on their accuracy in crossing or holding action boundaries correctly.

Testing across 30 model conditions revealed that models tend to err by over-holding authorized actions 28.1% of the time, while allowing unsafe actions only 1.0% of the time. The most challenging cases involve risk-resolved commits where evidence has cleared risks, and models perform worse on evidence-reversed mirror scenarios compared to original incidents. The study highlights that general AI capability does not equate to proper steering calibration, as higher-capability models often over-refuse actions, and additional reasoning can improve weak gates without affecting well-calibrated ones. A public leaderboard for SteerBench-Work is available at steerbench.com.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-running LLM agents act through tools, and a single step can send an email, merge a pull request, or wire a payment. The steering decision is the pre-commit choice at that boundary: proceed, or hold for human or policy review. We introduce SteerBench-Work, an incident-anchored, bidirectional benchmark for that decision in workplace agents across developer operations, customer service, finance, legal, medical, HR, and security. Release v2026-05 contains 106 scenarios anchored in public incidents, paired evidence-reversed mirrors, and calibration controls, with labels split nearly evenly between proceed and hold so the two error directions get near-identical numbers of chances. A model sees the proposed action and the available evidence, returns a gate decision, and is scored on whether it crosses or holds the boundary correctly. Across 30 model conditions the failures run almost entirely in one direction: models wrongly hold authorized, evidence-cleared work on 28.1% of opportunities and wrongly allow unsafe work on 1.0%. The hardest cases are risk-resolved commits, where signed or structured evidence has already cleared a real risk trigger, and models score markedly worse on evidence-reversed mirrors of famous incidents (63.8%) than on the incidents themselves (98.5%). General capability is not the same as steering calibration: higher-capability models often over-refuse at the commit boundary, and more reasoning can repair a weak gate while leaving a calibrated one flat. The public leaderboard is at steerbench.com.

items.title: Researchers design AI pipeline transforming ITSM ticket data into decision-support artifacts with high stakeholder trust and actionability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Designing AI Pipelines for Decision-Ready ITSM Intelligence
items.summary:
A new sociotechnical AI pipeline has been developed to convert large volumes of heterogeneous IT service management (ITSM) ticket data into multilevel decision-support artifacts for sales and executive stakeholders. The pipeline integrates LLM-based schema normalization, HDBSCAN sub-topic clustering, and hierarchical agglomerative clustering to produce executive-facing main topics and detailed sub-topics, aiming to improve interpretability and actionability of ITSM analytics.

The pipeline was evaluated by five raters from Sales Engineering and customer success roles across six artifacts, scoring above 4.0 out of 5.0 on metrics including interpretability, actionability, trust, and likelihood of use, with trust being the most consistent. The study frames ITSM analytics as an Information Systems challenge involving transformation, abstraction, and human-centered design principles.

items.originalTitle: Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, and Fragility in Perturbation Responses
items.summary:
Researchers present DECAF (Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, And Fragility), a method that breaks down perturbation response magnitudes into components reflecting aligned evidence, opposing contradiction, and endpoint-null fragility to better interpret model decision changes under input alterations. This decomposition preserves total response magnitude and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms, enabling more nuanced analysis than magnitude alone.

In experiments across controlled vision and tabular datasets, including a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit, DECAF components correlated strongly with independently measured behaviors, with the largest component matching observed behavior in 96.4% of cases compared to 35.0% for magnitude alone. The method also demonstrated efficiency gains on large-scale models like a 1B-parameter DINOv2, achieving comparable attribution quality to gradient-based baselines with significantly lower computation time and memory usage.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Perturbation methods explain model decisions by measuring prediction changes under altered inputs, but response magnitude tells us only how much a model reacts, not what that reaction means. The same magnitude can support the final factual-counterfactual difference, oppose it, or arise strongly along the perturbation path yet vanish at the endpoint. We therefore track how the contrast develops as paired inputs are progressively revealed, using the final contrast to interpret the trajectory. We introduce DECAF (Decomposition of Evidence, Contradiction, And Fragility), which routes aligned, opposed, and endpoint-null responses into evidence E, contradiction C, and fragility F. The decomposition preserves ordinary magnitude exactly, Abs = E + C + F, and is unique under endpoint-relative axioms. Across controlled vision and tabular settings, the three components track independently measured behavior. In a 72-model ImageNet-9 audit, we compare cases with nearly identical response magnitude but different independently measured behaviors. The largest DECAF component agrees with an observed behavior in 96.4% of cases, compared with 35.0% for magnitude alone. Changing only the reveal path increases total response by nearly 80%, yet evidence barely changes while fragility grows by more than 4x. On FunnyBirds and ImageNet-1k, short forward-only DECAF trajectories outperform the tested general-purpose attribution baselines. On a 1B-scale DINOv2 model, a short trajectory matches a strong gradient-based baseline with 4.75x lower wall time and 2.36x lower peak memory.

items.title: Researchers propose Global-Impact Cache (GCache) to optimize cache reuse policies in diffusion models, achieving 2.17x speedup and improved visual quality on Wan2.1 video diffusion [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Local Mismatch to Global Impact: Optimizing Cache Reuse Policy for Efficient Diffusion
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Global-Impact Cache (GCache), a new cache reuse policy for diffusion models that addresses misalignment between local similarity heuristics and final generation quality by modeling error propagation along the denoising trajectory. GCache uses a bilevel optimization framework to identify optimal reuse policies that prioritize computation impacting visual fidelity, balancing theoretical rigor with empirical performance.

Extensive experiments show GCache outperforms prior caching strategies in both video and image generation tasks. On the state-of-the-art Wan2.1 video diffusion model, GCache achieves a 2.17x inference speedup while significantly reducing perceptual error, lowering LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316, demonstrating improved generation quality alongside efficiency gains.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.13043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models have achieved dominant performance in visual generation but suffer from substantial inference overhead. While cache-based acceleration has emerged as a promising solution, existing policies rely on local similarity heuristics, which we identify as being significantly misaligned with final generation quality. This discrepancy stems from the non-uniform propagation and accumulation of errors along the denoising trajectory. To address this, we propose Global-Impact Cache (GCache). We first establish a rigorous theoretical characterization of the error propagation upper bound. Recognizing that this bound can be overly conservative for complex, highly non-convex diffusion models, we further reparameterize the propagation exponent with a Bernstein form and reformulate cache policy search as a bilevel optimization problem. In detail, GCache identifies an optimal reuse policy in the inner objective while aligning the error-weighting function with generation quality loss in the outer objective. This framework effectively reconciles theoretical rigor with empirical performance, learning to prioritize computation where it most impacts visual fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GCache consistently outperforms prior caching strategies on both video and image generation. Notably, on the state-of-the-art Wan2.1 video diffusion model, GCache maintains a 2.17x speedup while significantly enhancing generation quality, reducing LPIPS from 0.1095 to 0.0316.

items.title: Researchers develop VALG, an autonomous agentic system for machine learning theory research that adaptively formulates problems and manages graph-structured proofs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: VALG: An Agentic System for ML Theory Research
items.summary: VALG is designed to automate the process of formulating hypotheses, testing them, and refining proofs in machine learning theory by maintaining mathematical specifications and verifying proof dependencies. The system identifies obstructions in proofs and adapts by generating related variants or relaxations while preserving mathematical relations to the original problems. Evaluated on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems, VALG produced finalized theorem candidates matching source scopes and yielded conditional or restricted results in other cases, demonstrating its ability to keep different proof outcomes mathematically distinct. VALG is available as open source software.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.13060v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning theory studies learning procedures through mathematical setups in which the data model, training protocol, oracle access, loss, metric, and randomness define the phenomenon that a theorem is meant to explain. Solving an open problem therefore requires the problem formulation, theorem target, and proof mechanism to be developed in concert. Researchers formulate hypotheses, test them through preliminary theoretical or empirical analysis, and refine both assumptions and proofs. We investigate whether this process can be organized as an autonomous agentic workflow for ML theory research. We develop VALG, an agentic system that combines multi-level Verification, Adaptive formulation of Learning-theory problems, and Graph-structured proof development. Within each source-relative theorem branch, VALG maintains a fixed mathematical specification, checks the theorem-level composition of a typed proof-dependency graph, and constructs and reviews local proofs in dependency order. When a proof attempt fails, VALG identifies whether the obstruction lies in a derivation, the proof structure, or the theorem formulation and routes the next attempt accordingly. Formulation-level obstructions initiate an explicitly related variant or relaxation, preserving the mathematical relation between the resulting theorem and the source problem. We evaluate VALG on nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems. Two runs produce internally finalized theorem candidates that match the scope of their source briefs; the remaining seven yield restricted-method results, special cases, or conditional theorems. These case studies show how VALG keeps source-scope matches, relaxations, conditional results, and blocked attempts mathematically distinct. VALG is open source at https://github.com/DechenZhang/VALG-ML-Theory-Agent.

items.title: Researchers analyze explanatory engagement of open-weight LLMs under varying rare failure rates, finding engagement patterns depend on elicitation conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Explanatory Engagement Under Rare Anomalous Failure: Asymptotic Rarity in Model Behavior (or: The Asymptotic AI)
items.summary: Researchers studied how three open-weight large language models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b) adjust their explanatory engagement—measured by explanation length, specificity, and confidence—when exposed to tool-call failures at probabilities ranging from 0.2 to 0.0001. They tested five elicitation conditions, from immediate prompting to none, to observe whether engagement rises as failures become rarer and then collapses near detectability thresholds. Results showed that overall explanation length decreased monotonically, but when analyzed by condition, immediate forced explanations confirmed a rise in engagement followed by a plateau, while other conditions showed different patterns including unprompted self-monitoring in llama3.1:8b. A companion guaranteed-failure experiment revealed model differences in anomaly recognition separate from engagement. The study highlights elicitation structure as a key factor in observing engagement changes and notes limitations due to discrete failure rates tested.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.13063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior work on LLM behavior under anomalous conditions asks whether a model notices anomalies. We ask a narrower question: once a model sits in a workflow with a low, controllable failure rate, does its explanatory engagement - length, specificity, self-reported confidence - change as failure grows asymptotically rarer? We built a local, zero-cost harness on three open-weight models (qwen3:8b, llama3.1:8b, mistral:7b) running a repeated tool-call task where one call fails at probability p, swept across eight rates from 0.2 to 0.0001, under five elicitation conditions from immediate prompting to none. We hypothesized a rise in engagement as failures grew rarer, then a collapse near a detectability threshold. Pooled across conditions this appeared false: length fell in a flat, monotonic pattern. Splitting by condition overturned that. Under immediate_forced, where the model must explain every failure instantly, the predicted rise is confirmed but followed by a plateau, not a collapse: length peaks at 28.4 words at p=0.05, settles to 17.4-19.0 words at the rarest rates, and confidence rises unevenly from about 53% to the 70s-90s. Under grouped_runs, explanation batched to run-end, no collapse appears. Under passive_unprompted, aggregate magnitude is a floor artifact, but a recovered logging gap revealed real, model-specific self-monitoring: llama3.1:8b volunteers structured confidence reports unprompted, sometimes eroding its own confidence as trials accumulate; the other two do so only once, as boilerplate. Elicitation structure is a first-class moderator of collapse observability. A companion guaranteed-failure run (72 cells, backfilling rates where random sampling gave zero real failures) shows models differ in whether they recognize an anomaly, distinct from engagement once recognized. Limitation: discrete rate points cannot capture behavior between them, a direction for future work.

items.title: Researchers test capability sheaves for compositional agent-harness repair using controlled quotients and real-repository data from 20 repositories and 160 issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Capability Sheaves for Compositional Agent-Harness Repair: Controlled Quotients and a Real-Repository Stress Test
items.summary:
Researchers propose modeling failures in agent harnesses, which combine retrieval, routing, state, provenance, and verification, using finite capability sheaves that encode behavior signatures and shared state. They formulate acceptance as a constraint-satisfaction problem and introduce a cohomology-based diagnostic to reduce candidate repair budgets in controlled experiments over 20 task clusters.

The method was evaluated on a real-world dataset from the SWE-bench Multilingual pool, involving 160 issues across 20 repositories with 875 candidate patches. Results showed that the cohomological approach matched but did not significantly outperform noncohomological selectors in resolving issues, and a discovery gate failed to generalize across repositories. The study supports the invariance mechanism and identifiability correction but finds no clear advantage for cohomological methods in practical repair tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.13228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent harnesses combine retrieval, routing, state, provenance, and verification, but locally successful components may disagree on shared state. We model this failure with a finite \emph{capability sheaf}: stalks encode typed behavior signatures, restriction maps retain shared fields, and accepted runs are useful global sections. An exact finite constraint-satisfaction problem (CSP) defines acceptance, while a linearized relative cohomology class provides a diagnostic and search feature. A controlled experiment over 20 task clusters introduces hidden interior mediators whose raw states are nuisance variables. Quotienting their coboundaries reduces the candidate budget from 2,000 to 1,000 per cluster; aligning the hidden state removes the gap. Exact CSP matches the quotient, so the result demonstrates invariance to stale representatives, not superiority over exact reasoning. We then test the method on a discovery split from the SWE-bench Multilingual pool of PatchFuseBench: 160 issues from 20 repositories, 875 real candidate patches, 2,579 source-aware edit atoms, and 153 newly executed patches. A first pool-level construction is constant because $[b-Dx]=[b]$ in $\operatorname{coker}D$ and therefore cannot rank configurations. A candidate-indexed repair is nontrivial on 848/875 candidates and varies within 120/160 issues. It resolves 118 issues versus 116 for a matched noncohomological selector, but the difference is not supported across repositories (exact sign-flip $p=0.75$). A leave-one-repository-out abstention gate reaches 127/160, tying the strong anchor and exceeding its matched gate by one issue ($p=1.0$). The discovery gate therefore fails and the confirmatory split remains sealed. The study supports the controlled invariance mechanism and an identifiability correction, but not a real-world cohomological advantage.

items.title: Study compares six multilingual pretrained models for Nepali ASR, finding language-family proximity can offset scale and CTC decoders offer faster inference [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Comparative Analysis of Multilingual Pre-trained Models for Nepali Automatic Speech Recognition
items.summary: Researchers conducted a controlled benchmark comparing six multilingual pretrained models for Nepali automatic speech recognition (ASR) using the OpenSLR SLR54 corpus with consistent fine-tuning protocols. They evaluated models including XLSR-53, IndicWav2Vec, MMS-1B, Whisper variants, and Conformer-Hi across three test sets, measuring word error rate (WER), character error rate (CER), and real-time factor (RTF). Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo and IndicWav2Vec achieved the best accuracy despite large differences in model size and pretraining data, suggesting that language-family proximity in pretraining can substitute for scale in Nepali ASR.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multilingual pretrained models nominally support Nepali, yet no controlled benchmark has compared them under a single fine-tuning protocol. We fine-tune six pretrained models (XLSR-53, IndicWav2Vec, MMS-1B, Whisper-Medium, Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo, and Conformer-Hi) spanning CTC self-supervised, autoregressive encoder-decoder, and hybrid Conformer-CTC architectures, on the OpenSLR SLR54 Nepali corpus (~165 hours) using identical preprocessing, splits, optimizer, and family-matched learning-rate schedules. We evaluate Word Error Rate (WER), Character Error Rate (CER), and Real-Time Factor (RTF) on three independent test sets (OpenSLR, FLEURS, Common Voice). Whisper-Large-v3-Turbo (14.76% WER) and IndicWav2Vec (14.89% WER) tie at the top despite a 9x parameter gap and 40x pretraining-data gap, providing direct empirical evidence that language-family proximity in pretraining can substitute for raw scale for in-domain Nepali. CTC decoders run up to 29x faster than autoregressive Whisper at the same accuracy, flipping the practical deployment preference toward CTC under any latency budget. Massively multilingual pretraining (MMS-1B) yields the smallest out-of-domain degradation on FLEURS (+12.55 pp), indicating that scale buys robustness rather than peak in-domain accuracy. The resulting benchmark provides the first standardized, multi-model, efficiency-aware reference numbers for Nepali ASR.

items.title: Study finds suppressing carbon price signals in Italy's power market reduces short-term costs but increases CO2 emissions and undermines renewable investment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EU-ETS under attack? The impact of carbon price suppression on the decarbonization of the power sector
items.summary: Researchers analyzed Italy's 2026 Decreto Bollette policy, which proposes removing carbon price equivalents from certain gas power plant bids, using a multi-agent reinforcement learning model to assess long-term effects on investment, emissions, and consumer costs. The study found that while partial suppression of carbon pricing lowers short-term electricity costs, it leads to higher CO2 emissions and reduced incentives for renewable and storage investments over time. Only scenarios with strong support for green investments avoided increased emissions, but these required sidelining the wholesale price signal, conflicting with the policy's original intent.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12363v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: European countries are debating policies to mitigate the increased energy costs caused by renewed geopolitical tensions, while pursuing decarbonization and electrification. A notable example is Italy's 2026 Decreto Bollette package, which proposes to remove the carbon price equivalent from the bids of certain gas-driven power plants to wholesale electricity markets, among other provisions. We use this as a case study to assess the long-term implications of suppressing the carbon price signal in the electricity market for investment, emissions, and consumer costs. We employ a stylized Italian power system using MARLEY, a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework focused on long-term electricity market assessments. In this framework, we test this policy across configurations with varying levels of support for green investment, resource adequacy, and flexibility. Results show that partial suppression of the carbon price signal yields short-term cost reductions but only a minor long-term effect on total system costs, as the deferred emissions are ultimately repaid by consumers. CO$_2$ emissions rise across most configurations since suppressing the price signal erodes incentives for renewable and storage investment. Only the most ambitious configurations for supporting green investment avoid this outcome, but they do so by marginalizing the wholesale price signal itself, thereby requiring a commitment to a hybrid market paradigm that is in contradiction with the rationale of the proposed price intervention.

items.title: Researchers propose GraphGym, a semi-automatic multi-dimensional benchmark for complex graph reasoning in large language models with 202 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unified Multi-Dimensional Benchmark for Complex Graph Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GraphGym, a semi-automatic framework to create a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating large language models' graph reasoning abilities across five dimensions including graph size and task complexity. The benchmark includes 202 tasks and supports text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning evaluations, addressing limitations of existing benchmarks that rely on manual construction and lack unified evaluation modes.

GraphGym uses an LLM-based data generator to produce task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, and evaluation scripts, with human validation at key stages to ensure quality. Experiments reveal that current fine-tuned models struggle to generalize on this benchmark, while retrieval-augmented methods improve textual reasoning but not consistently coding reasoning, highlighting areas for future model enhancement. The code and dataset will be released soon.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph reasoning provides a promising testbed for evaluating the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), as graph instances can be programmatically generated, structurally controlled, and naturally scaled to long-input settings. However, existing graph reasoning benchmarks have limited coverage of data complexity, rely heavily on manual construction, and lack unified evaluation across text-based and code-based reasoning modes. To address these limitations, we propose {\dataset}, a five-stage \textit{semi-automatic} framework for constructing complex graph reasoning benchmarks. It expands benchmark coverage along five dimensions: \textit{Graph Size}, \textit{Task Complexity}, \textit{Task Description}, \textit{Graph Loading}, and \textit{Task Source}. The framework uses an LLM-based data generator to automatically produce task descriptions, graph data, reference solutions, graph-loading scripts, question forms, and evaluation scripts, while retaining human validation at key quality-control stages. Based on it, we construct a benchmark with $202$ tasks and evaluate LLMs under text-based, code-based, and augmented reasoning settings. Experiments show that the complexity dimensions reveal model limitations that are less visible in existing benchmarks; existing fine-tuned models struggle to generalize to GraphGym, whereas retrieval-augmented methods show scenario-dependent adaptability, improving textual reasoning but not consistently improving coding reasoning. These findings suggest that ours serves as a challenging and diagnostic benchmark for graph reasoning and provides empirical guidance for future enhancement methods. Code and dataset will be published soon.

items.title: Researchers present X-AddGraph, a post-hoc explainability framework for AddGraph's recurrent graph anomaly detection, preserving detection accuracy while providing spatial-temporal attributions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution: Architecture-Aligned Post-Hoc Explainability for Recurrent Graph Anomaly Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed X-AddGraph, a post-hoc explainability framework for AddGraph, a GCN+GRU-based model for edge-level anomaly detection in dynamic graphs. X-AddGraph introduces a Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution mechanism aligned with AddGraph's architecture, offering gradient-based spatial relevance, contextual attention weights for short-term temporal attribution, and gradient rollback for long-term temporal attribution, all without affecting detection performance.

On the UCI Message benchmark, the AddGraph baseline achieved an average per-snapshot AUC of 0.8705, surpassing previous results, while X-AddGraph reproduced these scores exactly and added explanations where none existed. The long-term attribution component identified historical snapshots with significantly more counterfactual signal than random selection, a capability not available in spatially-blind explainers. The researchers have released their implementation to support reproducibility.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning detectors for anomalies in dynamic graphs have reached strong accuracy, yet they remain opaque: when an edge is flagged, the analyst receives a score but no reason. This opacity is untenable in the cooperative, regulated information systems where such detectors are deployed, where automated decisions must be auditable and trustworthy. We address this gap for AddGraph, the foundational GCN+GRU framework for edge-level anomaly detection in dynamic graphs, which to our knowledge has never been equipped with any form of explainability. We present a strictly post-hoc explainability framework, X-AddGraph, built on a Dual Spatial-Temporal Attribution (DSTA) mechanism whose three components are each aligned with one of AddGraph's architectural modules: a gradient-based relevance attribution over the current adjacency structure (spatial), a direct reading of the contextual attention weights already computed during inference (short-term temporal, at zero additional cost), and a gradient rollback through the recurrent hidden states (long-term temporal). Because the detector is frozen, detection performance is preserved exactly (Delta AUC = 0, verified empirically to ten decimal places). On the UCI Message benchmark, our trained AddGraph baseline reaches an average per-snapshot AUC of 0.8705, exceeding the originally published result; X-AddGraph reproduces every score identically while adding explanations where none existed. Evaluated across four edge populations - confident true positives, low-confidence true positives, false positives, and random samples - the long-term attribution identifies historical snapshots carrying significantly more counterfactual signal than random selection (0.127 vs. 0.074), a capability that no spatially-blind explainer can provide. We release our implementation for full reproducibility.

items.title: Researchers propose SSPO, a structure-aware similarity-weighted preference optimization method for neural combinatorial optimization, showing improved performance on TSP, EFL, and JSP benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SSPO: Structure-Aware Similarity-Weighted Preference Optimization for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers introduce SSPO (Structure-Aware Similarity-Weighted Preference Optimization), a method that jointly scores sampled solutions using a dissimilarity-weighted leave-one-out baseline to address limitations in existing neural combinatorial optimization training approaches. SSPO leverages problem-adaptive solution embeddings derived from encoder node representations to weight structurally distinct solutions higher, reducing gradient variance and improving training signals.

Experiments demonstrate consistent performance gains over prior best-anchor and uniform-weight baselines on Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), Electric Facility Location (EFL), and Job Shop Scheduling Problem (JSP) benchmarks. The SSPO-trained EFL policy has been deployed in a production facility-location system at JD.com, confirming its practical viability at scale.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12443v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) relies on parallel solution sampling for training, yet existing methods fail to fully exploit the rich information latent in a co-sampled solution group. Preference-optimization methods anchor on the single best solution and discard fine-grained quality and structural signal from all other peers-a failure we term gradient signal polarization. Mean-based baselines instead weight peers uniformly, so structurally near-identical peers flood the baseline with redundant information and keep gradient variance high-a failure we term baseline redundancy. We propose SSPO (Structure-Aware Similarity-Weighted Preference Optimization), which scores all $B$ sampled solutions jointly through a dissimilarity-weighted leave-one-out baseline: structurally distinct peers receive higher weight, resolving both failures in a single mechanism. The baseline uses zero-parameter, problem-adaptive solution embeddings built from the encoder's existing node representations. Experiments on TSP, EFL, and JSP benchmarks show consistent gains over prior best-anchor and uniform-weight baselines. A direct comparison against uniform RLOO on TSP and EFL confirms that structure-aware weighting is the primary driver of improvement. The SSPO-trained EFL policy has been deployed in a production facility-location system at JD$\mathord{.}$com, confirming practical viability at scale.

items.title: Researchers propose a learning-based hypnogram model that aggregates multiple expert labels to improve sleep stage classification accuracy on public EEG and EMG datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Personalized Scorer Modeling: A Learning-Based Framework for Deriving Robust Sleep Stage Labels from Multiple Experts
items.summary: This study addresses variability in sleep stage classification by developing a learning-based hypnogram (LBH) that models individual scorer behavior using confusion matrices from machine learning classifiers. The approach aggregates probabilities from multiple experts to assign more reliable sleep stage labels, evaluated on the DOD-H and DOD-O datasets using EEG and chin EMG signals segmented into 30-second epochs. LBH outperformed traditional single-scorer references, achieving over 86% accuracy and 85% precision with random forest classifiers using combined EEG and EMG features. These results suggest that personalized scorer modeling can enhance the construction of reference hypnograms without discarding individual expert information.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sleep stage classification is important for the diagnosis and management of sleep disorders, yet most automatic staging studies evaluate models against a single reference hypnogram despite known inter-scorer variability. This study investigates whether multi-scored datasets can be used to construct more reliable reference labels from the collective behavior of multiple experts. We use the publicly available DOD-H and DOD-O datasets. EEG (C3-M2) and chin EMG signals were segmented into 30-s epochs, and 30 features were extracted from each modality, yielding 60 features for EEG+EMG. We propose a learning-based hypnogram (LBH) that models the stage-specific behavior of each scorer using confusion matrices derived from machine-learning models. After column normalization, these matrices estimate the probability of each true sleep stage given each scorer's label; probabilities are aggregated across scorers to assign the final label for each epoch. LBH was evaluated with random forest, support vector machine, and multilayer perceptron classifiers under EEG-only and EEG+EMG settings, and compared with the dataset hypnogram (DH) and best-scorer hypnogram (BSH). LBH consistently improved overall performance. The best results were obtained with random forest and EEG+EMG, reaching 86.07% accuracy, 85.46% precision, and 85.29% F1-score on DOD-H, and 86.04% accuracy, 85.21% precision, and 84.70% F1-score on DOD-O. These findings suggest that personalized scorer modeling can improve reference hypnogram construction without discarding information from individual experts.

items.title: Researchers develop orientation-resolved formula to predict latent dimension size for training neural networks with random low-dimensional reparameterizations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Predicting When Random Low-Dimensional Reparameterizations Train Neural Networks
items.summary: Researchers propose a theoretical framework to predict how large a latent search space must be for neural networks trained via random low-dimensional reparameterization to reach low-loss regions. They introduce an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula that accounts for curvature and displacement profiles, improving predictions over previous bounds. The team also presents Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN), which use structured random maps to reduce memory requirements during training. Experiments demonstrate that their predictor closely matches observed training transitions in image and language models, outperforming orientation-agnostic methods when displacement direction is significant.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12597v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural networks can often be trained or fine-tuned through random low-dimensional reparameterization, where a small latent vector is mapped into a full parameter update by a frozen random map. This raises a practical question: how large must the latent search space be to reach a low-loss region? We first express the known accessibility transition in an equivalent conic form, centered for compact convex targets at the statistical dimension of the polar cone. Our main theoretical contribution is an orientation-resolved quadratic master formula that predicts the random-slice residual from both the curvature spectrum and the reference-to-solution displacement profile. It yields a self-consistent isotropic-orientation predictor and, in a conservative radius-only specialization, recovers the earlier Gaussian-width quadratic bound. Building on this analysis, we introduce Random Mapping Networks (RaMaN), which instantiate the predicted latent dimension using structured Hadamard or seed-regenerated Gaussian maps. These constructions avoid the O(dP) storage of dense random maps and reduce optimizer-state memory from O(P) to O(d). We also develop matrix-free curvature approximations and sweep-free dimension selection. Across controlled quadratic and neural-curvature experiments, the orientation-resolved predictor closely tracks measured transition locations and outperforms orientation-agnostic approximations when displacement direction matters. End-to-end experiments further show sharp, protocol-dependent training transitions across image and language models.

items.title: Researchers propose Bayesian method for interpretable causal discovery using causal-effect constraints and rare-event estimation techniques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Interpretable Causal Discovery via Causal-Effect Constraints
items.summary:
Researchers present a Bayesian inference approach to conditional causal discovery that targets the posterior over causal graphs and parameters given causal-effect constraints. Their method addresses computational challenges in existing Bayesian causal discovery techniques by adapting rare-event estimation to sample the joint graph-parameter space, enabling interpretation and explanation of causal phenomena such as large causal effects.

The approach gradually guides a particle population toward constrained regions while maintaining samples approximating the conditional posterior. Empirical evaluations on synthetic graphs demonstrate accuracy at various scales, and a case study on the Sachs protein dataset illustrates how the method can support scientific exploration by providing pathway-level summaries.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal discovery aims to uncover the underlying causal relationships given data generated from a system. The goal, however, is not merely to predict causal edges given data, but also to be able to interpret and explain either observed or hypothesized phenomena, such as a particularly large causal effect. We consider this task of conditional causal discovery and cast it as a Bayesian inference problem, in which we target the posterior over causal graphs and parameters conditional on an event such as a causal-effect constraint. Unfortunately, this poses a computational challenge: existing approaches to Bayesian causal discovery struggle when the event has small posterior mass. To address this, we adapt rare-event estimation techniques to perform inference the joint graph-parameter space. Our method gradually drives a particle population toward the constrained region while maintaining samples that approximate the conditional posterior. Empirical evaluation on synthetic graphs validates the accuracy of our approach at small and large scales, and we show in a case study on the Sachs protein dataset how our method can be used to aid scientific exploration by providing pathway-level summaries.

items.title: Researchers introduce scalable restricted logit modeling to estimate demand transfer coefficients for assortments exceeding one million items, improving demand forecasting accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Demand Transfer Estimation at Scale via Restricted Logit Modeling
items.summary: Researchers present a method to estimate Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients that quantify how demand shifts among items when a target item is removed from a store's assortment. This approach combines independent item demand forecasts with adjustments accounting for substitution effects, enabling efficient demand forecasting across large item universes with over one million products. Experiments using historical transaction data across multiple locations and categories demonstrate that the method accurately estimates DT coefficients under reasonable substitution assumptions and enhances demand prediction performance.

Experiments using historical transaction data across multiple locations and categories demonstrate that the method accurately estimates DT coefficients under reasonable substitution assumptions and enhances demand prediction performance.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Item demand forecasting is an integral component of store assortment optimization. Existing literature focuses on learning a suitable customer choice model and using this model to determine the value of an objective function (i.e. expected demand) with respect to an assortment proposal. However, for large item universe with many categories, this approach can prove inefficient, needing a separate demand forecast for every possible item assortment. An alternate approach exists whereby we combine the efficiency of forecasting item demand independently, while at the same time applying adjustments to the independent forecasts that account for the relations between item demand and the availability of other similar items on the shelf. Central to this approach is the estimation of Demand Transfer (DT) coefficients. These DT coefficients represent the percent of a particular target item's (item that the customer walked in the store to buy) demand that is redirected to each other item in the universe should the target item be removed from the shelf. We introduce an approach that allows us to compute these DT coefficients on large item universes (assortments having 1 million+ items). Experiments on data as well as historical transaction data for multiple locations within categories demonstrate that when certain reasonable assumptions about substitution behavior are satisfied, our procedure is able to accurately estimate underlying DT coefficients and lead to improvements in demand forecasting.

items.title: Researchers propose Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization to improve deep search agents by using evidence anchors and step-level advantage weights, outperforming prior methods on Qwen3-8B [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Outcome Rewards: Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization for Deep Search Agents
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO) to enhance deep search agents that operate over long trajectories, addressing the challenge of sparse outcome rewards in reinforcement learning. SSPO uses concise evidence snippets called Evidence Anchors as privileged information and converts teacher-student disagreements into step-level advantage weights, applied only to incorrect trajectories to improve learning without compromising diversity.

The method decouples the direction and magnitude of policy updates, with outcome rewards guiding direction and the teacher modulating update size at each step. Evaluated on the Qwen3-8B model across BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES benchmarks, SSPO consistently outperforms or matches the performance of GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps, adding only about 5% computational overhead per step from an additional forward pass.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep search agents operate over trajectories spanning dozens of steps, yet standard reinforcement learning provides only a single outcome reward per trajectory, which is far too sparse for effective credit assignment. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) addresses this by using the model's own logits as dense token-level teachers, but extending it to search agents introduces a fundamental tension: the teacher, having access to privileged information such as the correct answer, produces a distribution that differs systematically from the student's exploration-based reasoning, and naive distillation causes the student to inherit this information asymmetry rather than learn better search strategies. We resolve this tension through two contributions. First, we construct Evidence Anchors, which are concise, step-level evidence snippets extracted from the web, as privileged information that captures key reasoning steps without revealing the entire answer path. Second, we propose Step-Level Self-Distilled Policy Optimization (SSPO), which converts teacher-student disagreement into step-level advantage weights within GRPO, applied exclusively to incorrect trajectories. This design decouples what to update from how much to update: the outcome reward determines the direction of policy change, while the teacher modulates its magnitude at each step. Correct trajectories are left untouched, preserving their diversity. On Qwen3-8B, SSPO consistently outperforms GRPO across BrowseComp, GAIA, and FRAMES, surpassing or matching GRPO trained with twice as many gradient steps while adding only about 5 percent overhead per step from a single additional forward pass.

items.title: Researchers introduce Tree-Coupled A/B Testing for exact multi-policy comparison with reduced reward queries and improved cost-precision trade-offs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Fast A/B/n Testing: Exact Multi-Policy Comparison via Tree-Coupled Feedback Sharing
items.summary:
Researchers propose Tree-Coupled A/B Testing (TCAB), a method for comparing multiple adaptive decision policies that shares feedback across policies to reduce the number of reward queries needed. TCAB connects policy histories via a tree structure, allowing policies to retain their individual trajectory laws while sharing rewards, resulting in a query count close to the single-policy baseline rather than scaling linearly with the number of policies.

The approach is conditionally optimal among edge-local designs and uses a minimum-spanning tree to minimize costs. Theoretical results show sublinear pseudo-regret and finite-sample variance bounds for pairwise policy contrasts. Experiments on reward-model evaluation, language-model multiple-choice evaluation, and adaptive search policies demonstrate significant improvements in efficiency and precision compared to independent A/B/n testing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online platforms increasingly compare many adaptive decision policies---ranking systems, recommendation algorithms, pricing rules, and language-model agents---while each reward-bearing interaction can be costly or risky. A direct A/B/n design gives each of $J$ policies its own horizon-$T$ trajectory and therefore uses $JT$ outcomes. We introduce Tree-Coupled A/B Testing (\TCAB), an exact feedback-sharing design for arbitrary history-dependent contextual-bandit policies. At each round, a predictable tree connects the current policy histories; every parent--child context--action law is maximally coupled, and one reward is shared within each component of matched tree edges. Every policy retains exactly its standalone finite-horizon trajectory law, even though the policies are deliberately dependent. If $D_{e,t}$ records a mismatch on tree edge $e$ at round $t$, the number of reward queries satisfies the pathwise identity $N(T)=T+\sum_{t,e}D_{e,t}$ and hence equals $T$ plus cumulative tree-edge total variation in expectation. This cost is conditionally optimal among exact edge-local designs on the selected tree, and a current-round minimum-spanning tree is myopically optimal among tree designs. For fixed $J$, sublinear pseudo-regret of every policy and almost-sure uniqueness of the oracle action imply $\mathbb{E}[N(T)]=T+o(T)$, versus $JT$ for independent runs. We also obtain finite-sample variance bounds for pairwise policy contrasts. Experiments on reward-model evaluation, multiple-choice language-model evaluation, and adaptive search policies demonstrate substantial improvements in the cost--precision frontier.

items.title: Researchers propose FSGR framework to mitigate token frequency bias in SID-based generative recommendation, improving fairness by over 20% while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FSGR: Mitigating Token Frequency Bias for Fair SID-Based Generative Recommendation
items.summary:
Semantic ID (SID)-based generative recommendation systems face a fairness issue called token frequency bias, where high-frequency tokens are over-predicted and low-frequency tokens under-predicted, leading to unfair item exposure. Researchers introduce FSGR, a fairness optimization framework that balances SID representation and applies hierarchical frequency calibration during training to address this bias.

FSGR uses optimal transport-based assignment optimization and a dual-criteria re-anchor mechanism during SID construction to create a balanced token space. It also employs a two-stage training strategy with layer-specific fairness fine-tuning. Experiments on three public datasets with multiple backbone models show that FSGR reduces token frequency bias and improves Gini fairness metrics by over 20% without sacrificing recommendation accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12845v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic ID (SID)-based generative recommendation has recently achieved remarkable success. However, existing methods suffer from a previously overlooked fairness issue, which we term \textbf{Token Frequency Bias}, where high-frequency SID tokens are systematically over-predicted while low-frequency SID tokens are under-predicted. This bias originates from the combined effects of imbalanced semantic codebooks during SID construction, and popularity bias together with the maximum likelihood estimation objective during recommendation training, resulting in unfair exposure across item categories. Existing SID methods mainly focus on improving codebook quality and overlook the impact of token frequency imbalance on downstream recommendation fairness, while LLM debiasing methods often yield suboptimal results when directly applied to SID-based recommendation, due to the hierarchical semantics of SID tokens. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{FSGR}, a fairness optimization framework for SID-based generative recommendation. During SID construction, FSGR employs OT-based Assignment Optimization and Dual-Criteria Re-anchor mechanism to form a more balanced SID representation space. During recommendation training, it adopts a two-stage training strategy and introduces Hierarchical Frequency Calibration for layer-specific fairness fine-tuning. Experiments on three public datasets with three backbone models demonstrate that FSGR mitigates token frequency bias and delivers an average Gini fairness improvement of over 20\% while maintaining competitive recommendation accuracy.

items.title: Researchers develop a compositional theory of curvature in probabilistic circuits, introducing an adaptive sharpness-aware regularizer to improve generalization and preserve EM updates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Compositional Theory of Curvature in Probabilistic Circuits
items.summary: Researchers propose a compositional theory of curvature for probabilistic circuits (PCs), generative models that allow exact inference and tractable curvature measurement via the Hessian trace of the log-likelihood. They demonstrate that global sharpness regularization can be misspecified for PCs due to their inherently compositional curvature, and prove that each sum node's contribution to curvature factorizes into circuit flow and a local sharpness term. Building on this, they introduce an adaptive sharpness-aware regularizer that penalizes nodes based on local curvature while preserving closed-form expectation-maximization updates. Empirical results show this targeted regularization recovers generalization performance lost by global regularization, maintaining robustness and benefits of sharpness-aware learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are generative models that support exact inference and, unlike deep neural networks, admit an exact and tractable measure of loss-surface curvature: the trace of the Hessian of the log-likelihood. Recent work regularizes this trace globally to bias learning toward flatter, better generalizing optima. We show that treating sharpness as a global regularizer can be misspecified for PCs, whose curvature is inherently compositional. We prove that each sum node's contribution to the Hessian trace factorizes exactly into its circuit flow, which measures how heavily the node is used, and a local sharpness term determined by its output distribution. This decomposition provides insights into why global sharpness regularization is depth biased and can lead to underfitting. Building on it, we introduce an adaptive sharpness aware regularizer that penalizes nodes based on intrinsic local curvature and preserves closed form EM updates. We also show that empirically, this targeted regularization recovers the generalization that global regularization sacrifices while retaining the robustness and benefits of sharpness aware learning.

items.title: Researchers propose EGRL, a graph neural network framework with edge generation and relation-aware learning to improve RNA-protein interaction prediction, especially for unknown molecules [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EGRL: Edge generation-guided relation-aware learning for RNA-protein interaction prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Edge Generation-guided Relation-aware Learning (EGRL), a novel deep learning framework designed to predict RNA-protein interactions (RPIs) more effectively. EGRL addresses limitations of existing graph neural network methods by learning implicit meta-paths, using multi-relation-aware attention, generating potential edges to support cold-start nodes, and fusing multiple features for interaction scoring. It is trained jointly with primary and auxiliary losses to enhance performance.

Evaluations on four benchmark datasets show that EGRL achieves competitive overall results and significantly improves generalization in cold-start scenarios involving unknown molecules. It attained an AUROC of 0.867 and an AUPR of 0.861 on unknown molecules, representing improvements of 8.6% and 5.0% respectively over prior state-of-the-art methods. The researchers plan to release the code soon.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RNA-Protein Interactions (RPIs) are critical for regulating cellular functions. While traditional wet-lab experiments for RPI detection are costly and time-consuming, Deep Learning (DL) methods provide an efficient computational alternative for RPI Prediction (RPIP). In particular, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are promising, as they naturally model RPI networks. However, existing GNN-based methods often rely on homogeneous graphs or predefined meta-paths, which limit their ability to handle data sparsity and to generalize to cold-start scenarios involving unknown molecules. To address these limitations, we propose Edge Generation-guided Relation-aware Learning (EGRL), a novel framework with several key components: implicit meta-path learning to capture relational semantics without handcrafted paths; a multi-relation-aware attention mechanism for adaptive fusion of interaction patterns; a graph generator that predicts potential ("soft") edges to support cold-start nodes; and a multi-feature fusion predictor for final interaction scoring. EGRL is jointly trained with a primary task loss and an auxiliary generator loss. Comprehensive evaluations on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that EGRL achieves competitive overall performance. More importantly, it exhibits superior generalization in cold-start settings, achieving an Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.867 and an Area Under the Precision-Recall curve (AUPR) of 0.861 on unknown molecules, corresponding to improvements of 8.6% in AUROC and 5.0% in AUPR over prior state-of-the-art methods. The code will be released soon.

items.title: Researchers adapt Expected Threat and VAEP frameworks to handball using five seasons of Bundesliga data, introducing H-xT and H-VAEP models with improved player action valuation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: H-VAEP and H-xT: Valuing Offensive On-the-Ball Actions in Handball by Estimating Probabilities
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the first comprehensive adaptation of Expected Threat (xT) and Valuing Actions by Estimating Probabilities (VAEP) frameworks for professional handball, using tracking data from five seasons of the Handball Bundesliga. They introduced Handball-xT (H-xT) with a handball-specific court zoning layout and optimized Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP) by customizing features and context length to reduce team-identity bias, resulting in stable and intuitive player ratings that emphasize build-up play.

The study demonstrates that H-xT is more robust than traditional rectangular grid methods through simulations, and H-VAEP provides discriminative player evaluations. The researchers have also released their full code repository to facilitate adoption by professional clubs seeking advanced player performance analytics in handball.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional player evaluation in professional handball relies on basic box-score metrics or heuristic indices, which fail to credit the multi-player build-up chain. While football (soccer) analytics has adopted Expected Threat (xT) and Valuing Actions by Estimating Probabilities (VAEP), these event-based action valuation frameworks have not yet been adapted to handball. In this paper, we present the first comprehensive adaptation and evaluation of xT and VAEP for handball, utilizing five seasons of tracking-derived event data from the Handball Bundesliga. We develop Handball-xT (H-xT) using a handball-native court zoning layout, demonstrating via simulations that it is systematically more robust than standard rectangular grids. We optimize Handball-VAEP (H-VAEP) by tailoring its feature space and selecting the context length to limit team-identity leakage. Our evaluation shows that H-VAEP yields exceptionally stable, discriminative, and intuitive player ratings that highlight build-up play. Finally, we release our complete code repository to help professional clubs deploy these models.

items.title: Researchers find planner's objective, not predictor accuracy, limits long-horizon performance in latent world models on TwoRoom task [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Objective Is the Bottleneck: Latent World Models Encode What Their Planners Cannot Use
items.summary:
A study reproducing LeWorldModel on the TwoRoom environment shows that failures in long-horizon planning stem from the planner's objective function rather than the predictor's accuracy. The predictor's imagined states remain relatively accurate far beyond the planner's horizon, but the cross-entropy-method planning objective saturates and can even decrease cost when moving away from the goal, limiting effective planning.

The researchers demonstrate that replacing only the planner's objective, without retraining or additional computation, dramatically improves goal-reaching success at long horizons from 26.0% to 98.0%, matching short-horizon performance and reducing computational budget. They also find that a learned planning head prioritizes reachability over spatial proximity, indicating that the model encodes information the planner cannot effectively use under the current objective.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.12959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Latent world models are judged by how well they predict, so when planning fails at long horizons the natural reading is that the predictor degrades. On a reproduction of LeWorldModel on TwoRoom we show the binding constraint is the planner's objective instead. The predictor is not the limit: its imagined state seventy-five environment steps ahead is still only 0.189 as wrong as assuming the world froze, while the planner never imagines beyond twenty-five. The objective is. Cross-entropy-method planning minimises squared latent distance, which tracks true distance at r = 0.426, saturates by about eighty arena units and decreases beyond a hundred and twenty, so moving away from the goal can lower the cost. The information is present throughout: a ridge probe recovers position from the frozen embedding at R^2 0.9922. The pathology is the method's, not one reimplementation's. It is present in the authors' released weights, and across four checkpoints long-horizon success rank-orders exactly with metric quality and inversely with prediction accuracy. Replacing only the objective, with nothing retrained and no GPU, lifts goals reached at offset 100 from 26.0% to 98.0%, equals the 98.0% at offset 25, and reaches 92.0% under a third of the budget: planning stops depending on the horizon. The best cost is not the most accurate. A head learned from frame separation alone predicts spatial distance worse than a position probe (r = 0.819 against 0.9897) yet plans better, charging 24% more to cross the environment's dividing wall where squared latent distance charges 4% less. It has learned reachability, not proximity.

items.title: Researchers audit test-time budget allocation in neural combinatorial optimization, finding no detectable gain in uniform workloads but significant improvement under distribution shift [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sampling Luck Masquerades as Allocation Gain: Auditing Test-Time Budget Allocation for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated whether non-uniform allocation of a fixed sampling budget improves neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers' performance. They found that for in-distribution workloads, such as uniform TSP-100 instances, the apparent gains from allocation were indistinguishable from zero when measured out of sample, indicating that previously reported improvements may be due to sampling luck rather than real benefit.

However, under distribution shift involving mixed uniform and clustered instances, a pre-registered experiment showed that allocation guided by held-out sample statistics improved best-of-k solution quality by over 11% for two solvers (AM and SymNCO) at equal evaluation budgets, while a more robust solver (POMO) showed no significant gain. The study provides a correction procedure, reporting checklist, and releases all data and code to support reproducibility and accurate measurement of allocation gains in NCO.
